title: Content with what comes
hook: contentment isn't getting what you want but wanting what comes (Discourses 1.12)

segments.voice: Yesterday: love stays, the father who ran from the sickroom, and your line, an ordinary chair pulled up beside a bed. Was there someone you stayed with a little longer? Day three hundred ninety-eight.

A child learning to write her name sometimes wants to spell it her own way. An extra letter here, a backward one there, because she likes how it looks. The teacher gently says no: your name is spelled like this. And at some point the child stops fighting it, and starts wanting to write it the way it really is. Epictetus suspected plenty of adults are still at the stage of the backward letter, with their whole lives. Today: content with what comes.
screen: `SPELLING YOUR NAME YOUR OWN WAY.` → `IT'S SPELLED LIKE THIS.` → `WANTING IT AS IT IS.`

segments.voice: Discourses book one, chapter twelve, is on contentment. Epictetus starts with a survey of what people believe about the gods. Some say there are none. Some say they exist but do nothing. Some say they care for the heavens but not for us. Some say they care for us, but only in general. And some, like Socrates, say they're aware of every move we make. He sides with the last, and builds on it. If the world is ordered by reason, then being educated, he says, means learning to want things to happen as they actually do happen. That's the radical line. Not getting what you want. Wanting what comes. And then the writing lesson. When I learn to write a name, he says, I don't get to spell it however I like. I learn to want it the way it is. Same with music. Same, he says, with life. Isn't that just giving up? Epictetus says no, and here's his surprising example. Socrates sat in prison, but he wasn't imprisoned, because he was there willingly. A prison, for Epictetus, is a place you're held against your will. Take away the against, and the walls are just walls. Not everyone accepts the Stoic picture of a reasoning universe behind events, and Epictetus himself lists those who don't. But his practice can be tried by anyone: stop fighting the spelling of the day, and see what changes.
screen: `WHAT PEOPLE BELIEVE ABOUT THE GODS.` · `WANT THINGS AS THEY HAPPEN.` · `LEARNING TO SPELL A NAME.` · `SOCRATES, NOT IMPRISONED.` · then, large: `CONTENT.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Think of one thing that came today that you didn't choose: the weather, a delay, a mood in the house, an ache. Notice the small push against it, the part of you spelling it your own way. Now try, just for a few breaths, to want it as it is. Not to like it. To stop pushing. If the push comes back, that's fine. Notice it, and let it go again. The bell holds the time.
Content with what comes. Epictetus' definition of an education: learning to want things to happen as they actually happen, the way a child learns her name's real spelling.
Your line: content. Pick one thing that came today without asking you, and try wanting it, just as it is, for one hour. Day three hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners take one unchosen event of the day, a delay or a disappointment, and rehearse wanting it as it is rather than as they wished it to be.

what a scholar hears: the Stoic ideal of 'living in agreement with nature' sits behind this; Epictetus defines education itself as bringing your will into line with how events unfold.
